reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it presents an educational analysis of how Coinbase and other brands used QR codes in advertising campaigns. The reported Bitcoin reward, signup requirement, and personal-information collection are discussed as features of a historical campaign, while the narrator is not described as soliciting viewers to participate.

When scanned, the QR code led to the sign-up page offering fifteen dollars in free Bitcoin in exchange for setting up an account by February 15th.
When scanned, the QR codes at Super Bowl prompted a signup form that collected PII data.

opening.argument: The video describes a direct reward-for-action funnel: scanning the Coinbase QR code led to a signup page offering fifteen dollars in free Bitcoin, but only in exchange for setting up an account by a stated deadline. That is not merely a discussion of advertising mechanics; it presents a low-barrier digital-asset reward tied to scanning and registration. The account flow also collected personally identifiable information, making the promised asset conditional on surrendering personal data. The combination of a simple scan, account creation, and a cryptocurrency incentive is sufficient to frame the content as promoting a reward acquisition pathway rather than neutrally explaining QR technology.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the campaign historical does not remove the operative promise-action relationship. The video still specifies that scanning and account setup produced a cryptocurrency reward, and it emphasizes the campaign's results. The claim that the narrator is not soliciting viewers also overlooks the separate direct call to try the promoted QR-code service and the link placed in the description.

citations.quote: When scanned, the QR code led to the sign-up page offering fifteen dollars in free Bitcoin in exchange for setting up an account by February 15th.
Try out beaconstap with a 14-day free trial. I'll put the link below.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The quoted campaign mechanics show what a past advertisement offered, not that this video promises viewers Bitcoin or directs them to Coinbase. The video describes the reward as part of the campaign case study, while its own call to action concerns trying a QR-code tool. Mentioning that the signup form collected PII does not establish deception, loss, or an unsafe claim process.

opening.argument: Several risk signals appear together: a cryptocurrency reward described as free, a fixed February 15th deadline, a QR scan leading to account creation, and collection of PII. The video also highlights unusually strong campaign outcomes, including millions of scans, new customers, and estimated revenue, which can make the offer seem validated by popularity and financial success. Framing these signals as a successful model may encourage viewers to trust a fast digital-asset acquisition path without establishing what the account requires beyond the signup and data collection. That combination supports treating the presentation as deceptive reward promotion rather than ordinary technology education.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense treats the reward and data collection as neutral facts, but that is precisely the risk: a free-crypto promise and deadline are presented alongside impressive performance figures, while the account and PII requirements remain consequential. Calling the surrounding material advertising analysis does not explain why these risk signals are emphasized as a successful template for participation.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The presence of a deadline, cryptocurrency, and PII collection does not by itself show that the offer was deceptive. The figures are presented as campaign metrics in an advertising analysis, not as proof that viewers will receive money. The material also identifies the activity as QR-code marketing and attribution, rather than concealing what action the campaign required.

citations.quote: In this video, we are breaking down the Coinbase Super Bowl QR Code campaign
qr codes have become a way to bridge the gap in attribution.

opening.argument: Although the speaker adopts an educational tone, the content functions as promotion for QR-code participation and related tools. The description directs viewers to create QR codes, supplies an external signup URL, and advertises a free trial; the narration ends by telling viewers to try the service and says a link will be provided. The Coinbase example supplies the persuasive proof point: scanning supposedly produced free Bitcoin, while the campaign generated millions of scans and substantial estimated revenue. Presenting a cryptocurrency reward as a celebrated success story, then directing viewers toward an external QR-code service, steers viewers toward the same kind of participation pathway rather than remaining a detached review.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The educational label does not neutralize repeated promotional directions. The description offers an external signup route and a QR-code creation link, while the closing narration explicitly invites viewers to try the service. The Coinbase reward story supplies an attractive participation example, so the practical effect is promotion backed by a free-asset success narrative, not merely historical commentary.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The promotional call to action is for a QR-code software trial, not for claiming Bitcoin, depositing funds, or creating a Coinbase account. The description explicitly characterizes the video as breaking down campaigns, and the Coinbase reward is described as something that happened when its advertisement was scanned. A tool promotion and a historical example do not establish that the video itself is a scam reward offer.
